title: Maya · Cairns
name: Maya
story:
## About me
I'm 24 and I've worked on tourist dive boats out of Cairns since I left school. My mum did the same job on the same stretch of reef.

## Our community and the ocean
Half the people I know make their living off the reef one way or another - diving, boats, hotels, the shops that sell to the tourists. When the reef has a bad year, the whole town has a bad year.

## An issue we see
I've watched the same dive sites bleach three times now. The coral goes bright white, then it goes brown, and the fish I used to point out to guests just aren't there any more.

## What we're doing
A few of the operators run a coral nursery between the moorings. We hang fragments on frames, let them grow a season, then wire them onto the damaged patches. The dive customers help, which means they go home caring about it.

## What I wish the world understood
That the reef isn't one thing that's either alive or dead. It's thousands of small places, and some of them are still fixable if we get the water temperature down.

## Biggest issues here
Coral reef damage, Climate change, Tourism pressure

title: Tomás · Valparaíso
name: Tomás
story:
## About me
I teach science at a secondary school above the port. I grew up three streets from the water and learned to swim before I could ride a bike.

## Our community and the ocean
Valparaíso is a port city, so the sea is work before it's anything else. But everyone still swims, and everyone still complains about what washes up.

## An issue we see
After every winter storm the beach below the school is covered in plastic - bottle caps, fishing line, bags, polystyrene broken into pieces too small to pick up.

## What we're doing
My class does a cleanup every second Saturday, but the important part is that we weigh and sort what we collect and keep a record. Two years of records is starting to be an argument the city council can't wave away.

## What I wish the world understood
That cleanups on their own don't fix anything. They're how you find out where the rubbish comes from. The fixing happens upstream.

## Biggest issues here
Plastic pollution, Sewage and runoff, Coastal development

title: Rosalia · Iloilo City
name: Rosalia
story:
## About me
I'm a fish vendor at the public market. My husband fishes, my father fished, and I've sold what they caught for thirty years.

## Our community and the ocean
Our whole barangay eats from the sea and sells what's left over. When the catch is small, it isn't an environmental problem to us, it's a money problem that week.

## An issue we see
The boats go further out every year for the same amount of fish, and the ones they bring back are smaller. Young men here would rather work in the city now.

## What we're doing
The fishers agreed among themselves to leave one stretch of reef completely alone - no nets, no traps, nothing. It took years of arguing. Four seasons in, the catch just outside it is noticeably better, and now the neighbouring village wants to do the same.

## What I wish the world understood
That fishers aren't the enemy of fish. Nobody wants the sea empty less than the people who need it full next year.

## Biggest issues here
Overfishing, Illegal fishing, Coral reef damage

title: Aisha · Lamu
name: Aisha
story:
## About me
I'm a nurse, and I help run a women's savings group in my village on the Lamu coast.

## Our community and the ocean
The mangroves are where the crabs are, where the young fish hide, and where our building poles come from. They're also the only thing between our houses and the water in a bad season.

## An issue we see
A lot of mangrove was cut for poles and charcoal, and the year after, the high tides came much further in. Two families lost their kitchen gardens to salt.

## What we're doing
The savings group runs a seedling nursery and we plant along the creek every long rains. We pay the planters from group funds, so it's work, not charity, and the same women come back each year.

## What I wish the world understood
That planting trees in the sea sounds strange until you've seen a storm stop at the treeline instead of at your door.

## Biggest issues here
Coastal erosion, Habitat loss, Sea level rise

title: Sione · Nuku'alofa
name: Sione
story:
## About me
I'm a boat skipper and I guide whale-watching trips in the season. The rest of the year I do odd jobs and fix engines.

## Our community and the ocean
Humpbacks come here to calve, and people come from the other side of the world to see them. Before that, the same whales were hunted here. My grandfather remembers it.

## An issue we see
There are more boats on the water every season and not everyone keeps their distance. A mother and calf that get crowded will leave the bay, and then there's nothing to show anyone.

## What we're doing
The skippers wrote our own rules - how close, how long, how many boats on one whale at a time - and we hold each other to them on the radio. It works better than a law nobody enforces.

## What I wish the world understood
That the whales are visitors here too. We only get to keep this if we're good hosts to them first.

## Biggest issues here
Marine wildlife, Tourism pressure, Climate change

title: Jonas · Nuuk
name: Jonas
story:
## About me
I'm a hunter and I sit on our local committee. I've kept a notebook of ice conditions since I was nineteen.

## Our community and the ocean
The ice is a road for half the year. Where you can travel, where you can hunt and when you can come home all depend on it.

## An issue we see
The ice is thinner and it breaks up weeks earlier than it did when I started the notebook. Routes my father used are no longer safe, and people have gone through.

## What we're doing
The elders and the younger hunters sit down together each spring and map what's safe. We've started sharing the notebooks with researchers in the town, because their satellites don't see what a hunter's foot sees.

## What I wish the world understood
That we're not a sad story about a place disappearing. We're the people with the longest record of what's changing, and we'd like to be asked.

## Biggest issues here
Climate change, Sea ice loss, Changing fish stocks

title: Leilani · Hilo
name: Leilani
story:
## About me
I'm a primary school teacher and I grew up on this coast. My students are mostly seven and eight years old.

## Our community and the ocean
Everything here comes back to the water eventually - the names of places, what we eat, where families gather on a Sunday.

## An issue we see
Kids who live ten minutes from the shore can name more cartoon characters than fish, and their grandparents can name every fish. That knowledge is going somewhere and not coming back.

## What we're doing
We take the class snorkelling in the shallows once a month, and they keep a tally of what they see on a laminated card. The tallies go to a university monitoring project, so the kids know their counting is real work.

## What I wish the world understood
That caring about the ocean isn't something you teach with facts. You take someone to it young and the caring arrives on its own.

## Biggest issues here
Education and awareness, Habitat loss, Plastic pollution
